title: Organic Fuels: Petroleum, Alkanes & Alkenes
description: Displayed and molecular formulae, homologous series, functional groups and general formulae; petroleum fractional distillation and the uses of its fractions; alkane combustion; cracking and the bromine-water test for IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: Molecular and Displayed Formulae
notes.body:
0620 Paper 2 and Paper 4 both ask you to READ and DRAW organic structures, so the first skill is telling the formula types apart.

📌 Definitions
• A **molecular formula** shows the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule: butane is C₄H₁₀. It tells you nothing about how the atoms are arranged.
• A **displayed formula** shows every atom AND every bond in the molecule, with each covalent bond drawn as a line. The displayed formula of methane shows one C joined by four single lines to four H atoms.

🔑 How it works
In a displayed formula every carbon atom must have exactly FOUR bond lines leaving it, every hydrogen exactly ONE, and every oxygen exactly TWO. Examiners deduct a mark for every carbon with three or five bonds — count around each atom before you finish.

💡 Worked Example
Ethanol has the molecular formula C₂H₆O. Its displayed formula shows C–C–O chains: the first carbon carries three C–H bonds, the second carbon carries two C–H bonds plus the C–O bond, and the oxygen carries the O–H bond. Counting atoms from the drawing gives 2 C, 6 H and 1 O — matching C₂H₆O.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a molecular formula when the question says 'draw the displayed formula'. C₂H₄ scores nothing if the examiner asked for every bond shown — you must draw H₂C=CH₂ with both lines of the double bond.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Molecular formula = atom count only; displayed formula = every atom and every bond.
• A double bond is drawn as TWO parallel lines (C=C), not one thick line.

notes.heading: Homologous Series and Functional Groups
notes.body:
Organic chemistry looks enormous until you realise the exam only tests a few FAMILIES of compounds that behave predictably.

📌 Definitions
• A **homologous series** is a family of compounds with the same functional group, similar chemical properties, and neighbouring members that differ by a CH₂ unit. Alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids are the four series in 0620.
• A **functional group** is the atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic reactions: C=C for alkenes, –OH for alcohols, –COOH for carboxylic acids.

🔑 How it works
Members of one series share the same general formula and trend in physical properties: as the chain lengthens, boiling point and viscosity increase and flammability decreases. Chemically they all react the same way, because the functional group — not the chain length — controls the reactions.

💡 Worked Example
Methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆) and propane (C₃H₈) are consecutive members of the alkane series: each differs from the last by CH₂, and all three burn in oxygen the same way.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying members of a homologous series have 'the same chemical formula'. They do not — each member has its own molecular formula. What they share is the functional group and the general formula.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Functional group decides the chemistry; chain length decides the physical trend.
• Neighbouring members of a series differ by CH₂.

notes.heading: General Formulae of the Four Families
notes.body:
The general formula lets you write the molecular formula of ANY member of a series from its carbon number alone — a reliable one-mark question.

📌 The four general formulae (Core)
• Alkanes: **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂** — e.g. n = 1 gives CH₄ (methane).
• Alkenes (one C=C bond): **CₙH₂ₙ** — e.g. n = 2 gives C₂H₄ (ethene).
• Alcohols: **CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH** — e.g. n = 2 gives C₂H₅OH (ethanol).
• Carboxylic acids: **CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH** — e.g. n = 1 gives CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid).

💡 Worked Example
What is the molecular formula of the alkane with 8 carbon atoms? Use CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 8: hydrogen atoms = (2 × 8) + 2 = 18, so the formula is C₈H₁₈ (octane).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and CₙH₂ₙ. The alkane has TWO MORE hydrogens than the alkene with the same number of carbons — the alkene 'lost' two hydrogens when the double bond formed. Check: butane C₄H₁₀ vs butene C₄H₈.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; alkenes CₙH₂ₙ; alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH; carboxylic acids CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH.
• Given any carbon number, substitute for n and count carefully.

notes.heading: Petroleum and Fractional Distillation
notes.body:
Petroleum (crude oil) is the raw material for almost every fuel in this topic, and separating it is a favourite long-answer question.

📌 Definition
Petroleum is a **mixture of hydrocarbons** — compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. Because it is a mixture, not a compound, its components can be separated by physical means using their different boiling points.

🔑 How fractional distillation works
1. Crude oil is heated to about 400 °C so that most of it vaporises.
2. The vapour enters the bottom of a tall **fractionating column** that is hot at the bottom and cooler towards the top.
3. As the vapour rises it cools. Each fraction condenses at the height where the column temperature matches its boiling point, and is tapped off.
4. Long-chain hydrocarbons with high boiling points condense near the bottom; short-chain molecules with low boiling points leave as gases at the top.

📌 Property trend up the column
From bottom to top the fractions show: decreasing boiling point, increasing volatility, decreasing viscosity (they flow more easily), and decreasing chain length. Exam questions often ask you to USE this trend to place a new fraction.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the column 'burns' or 'reacts' the oil. Fractional distillation is a PHYSICAL separation — no chemical reaction happens in the column.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Petroleum = mixture of hydrocarbons; separated by fractional distillation.
• High in the column = small molecules, low boiling point, very volatile.

illustration.alt: A fractionating column separating heated crude oil into fractions: refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene and diesel leave at successively lower levels, fuel oil drains lower and bitumen collects at the hot bottom, with the use of each fraction labelled.
illustration.caption: Fractional distillation of petroleum: small, low-boiling molecules leave near the cool top; bitumen stays at the hot bottom.

notes.heading: The Fractions and Their Uses
notes.body:
0620 expects you to name each fraction AND match it to its use — learn them as pairs, in column order.

📌 The fractions, top to bottom
• **Refinery gas** — bottled gas for heating and cooking.
• **Petrol (gasoline)** — fuel for cars.
• **Naphtha** — feedstock for making chemicals in the chemical industry.
• **Kerosene (paraffin)** — fuel for jet aircraft.
• **Diesel oil (gas oil)** — fuel for diesel engines (lorries, buses, trains).
• **Fuel oil** — fuel for ships and for home heating systems.
• **Bitumen** — surfacing roads.

🔑 How to remember the order
The order follows the property trend: the smaller the molecules, the lower the boiling point and the higher up they are collected. Refinery gas has the smallest molecules (1–4 carbons); bitumen has the largest (long chains and waxes).

💡 Worked Example
A fraction condenses just below kerosene and is used in lorry engines. Just below kerosene in the column sits diesel oil — matching 'diesel engines'. The position and the use agree, as they must.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping naphtha and kerosene. Naphtha is the chemical-industry feedstock (it is later cracked to make alkenes); kerosene is the jet fuel.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Order top to bottom: refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen.
• Every fraction has a named use — examiners pair them up in matching questions.

notes.heading: Alkanes as Fuels: Complete and Incomplete Combustion
notes.body:
Alkanes are generally unreactive, but they all burn — that is why the petroleum fractions are fuels.

📌 Complete combustion (plenty of oxygen)
An alkane burns in a plentiful oxygen supply to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy:
**methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

📌 Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen)
When the oxygen supply is restricted — a blocked gas flame, a car engine, a fire in a closed room — the carbon is not fully oxidised. The products are **carbon monoxide** (CO) and water, or even soot (particles of carbon, C) and water. Less energy is released than in complete combustion.

🔑 Why it matters
Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless, TOXIC gas: it binds to haemoglobin in the blood and stops oxygen being carried. This is why gas appliances need ventilation and why the exam loves the phrase 'limited supply of oxygen'.

💡 Worked Example
Propane burns completely: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Check the atoms: 3 C and 8 H on each side; oxygen: 5 × 2 = 10 on the left and (3 × 2) + 4 = 10 on the right.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing hydrogen (H₂) as a combustion product. The hydrogen in a hydrocarbon always ends up in WATER — never as H₂ gas.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Complete combustion: CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete: CO (or C) + H₂O, less energy.
• CO is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin.

notes.heading: Alkenes, Cracking and the Bromine-Water Test
notes.body:
Alkenes are the reactive cousins of the alkanes — everything in this note traces back to the C=C double bond.

📌 Definitions
• An **alkene** is a hydrocarbon whose molecules contain one carbon–carbon double bond, C=C. The C=C bond is the functional group, so alkenes are **unsaturated** — two more hydrogen atoms could still be added across the double bond.
• A **saturated** hydrocarbon (an alkane) contains only single C–C bonds and holds the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.

🔑 Cracking — making alkenes
Crude oil contains too many long-chain alkanes (low demand) and not enough petrol-range molecules and alkenes (high demand). **Cracking** breaks long-chain alkane molecules into shorter, more useful molecules:
• Conditions: the vapour is passed over a **heated catalyst**.
• Products: a shorter alkane plus an **alkene** (and sometimes hydrogen).
• Why: the short alkanes boost petrol supply, and the alkenes are the feedstock for making polymers and other chemicals.

🔑 The bromine-water test
Shake the unknown hydrocarbon with orange **aqueous bromine**:
• Unsaturated compound (C=C present): the bromine reacts with the double bond — colour changes from **orange to colourless**.
• Saturated compound (single bonds only): **no change** — the mixture stays orange.
This is the standard 0620 test for distinguishing an alkene from an alkane.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Describing the result as 'the bromine goes clear because it is diluted'. The colour disappears because bromine is USED UP reacting with the C=C bond — it is a chemical change, not dilution.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Cracking = heated catalyst; long alkane → short alkane + alkene.
• Bromine water: alkene turns it orange → colourless; alkane leaves it orange.

flashcards.definition: A formula showing the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule, with no information about how the atoms are arranged.
flashcards.example: Butane is C₄H₁₀ — four carbons and ten hydrogens, arrangement unknown.

flashcards.definition: A formula showing every atom and every bond in a molecule, with each covalent bond drawn as a line.
flashcards.example: Ethene is drawn as H₂C=CH₂ with both lines of the C=C double bond shown.

flashcards.definition: A family of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which neighbouring members differ by a CH₂ unit.
flashcards.example: Methane, ethane and propane are consecutive members of the alkane series.

flashcards.definition: The atom or group of atoms in an organic molecule that gives the compound its characteristic chemical reactions.
flashcards.example: The –OH group makes ethanol an alcohol; C=C makes ethene an alkene.

flashcards.definition: Describes a hydrocarbon in which all the carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds, so each carbon holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms.
flashcards.example: Alkanes such as propane, C₃H₈, are saturated.

flashcards.definition: Describes a hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C), so more hydrogen atoms could still be added.
flashcards.example: Ethene, C₂H₄, is unsaturated and decolourises bromine water.

flashcards.definition: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.
flashcards.example: For octane n = 8, so the formula is C₈H₁₈.

flashcards.definition: CₙH₂ₙ for alkenes with one C=C double bond — two fewer hydrogens than the alkane with the same carbon number.
flashcards.example: For hexene n = 6, so the formula is C₆H₁₂.

flashcards.definition: The physical separation of petroleum (a mixture of hydrocarbons) into fractions by their different boiling points, using a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top.
flashcards.example: Low-boiling fractions such as refinery gas leave at the top; bitumen stays at the bottom.

flashcards.definition: Breaking long-chain alkane molecules into shorter alkanes and alkenes by passing the vapour over a heated catalyst.
flashcards.example: Cracking heavy fractions increases the supply of petrol and of alkenes for polymer manufacture.

flashcards.definition: Complete combustion (plenty of oxygen) gives carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) gives toxic carbon monoxide or soot, plus water, and less energy.
flashcards.example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O is complete; a yellow, sooty Bunsen flame is incomplete.

flashcards.definition: The test for unsaturation: an unsaturated compound (C=C) turns orange aqueous bromine colourless; a saturated compound leaves it orange.
flashcards.example: Hexene decolourises bromine water; hexane does not.

choices: A set of compounds with identical molecular formulae but different names
A family of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which neighbouring members differ by CH₂
A mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation
A row of the periodic table containing the elements carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
questions.explanation: A homologous series shares one functional group, one general formula and similar chemistry, with consecutive members differing by CH₂. Identical molecular formulae would describe isomers, not a series.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a displayed formula?
choices: It shows only the number of each type of atom in the molecule
It shows the arrangement of electrons in the outer shell of each atom
It shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms
It shows every atom and every bond in the molecule, with each bond drawn as a line
questions.explanation: A displayed formula draws every atom and every covalent bond as a line. Atom counts alone give the molecular formula, and the simplest ratio is the empirical formula.

questions.stem: What is the molecular formula of the alkane with 8 carbon atoms?
questions.explanation: Use the alkane general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 8: hydrogens = (2 × 8) + 2 = 18, giving C₈H₁₈ (octane). C₈H₁₆ would be the alkene formula CₙH₂ₙ.

questions.stem: Which is the general formula of the alkenes that contain one C=C double bond?
questions.explanation: Alkenes have two fewer hydrogen atoms than the corresponding alkane, so the general formula is CₙH₂ₙ. CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is for alkanes and CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH for alcohols.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon is described as saturated. What does this mean?
choices: It contains at least one C=C double bond
All its carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds, so it holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms
It contains oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen
questions.explanation: Saturated means every carbon–carbon bond is single — no more hydrogen can be added across a multiple bond. A C=C bond would make the compound unsaturated.

choices: A solution of carbon dioxide in water
An element formed from compressed plant material
questions.explanation: Petroleum (crude oil) is a mixture of hydrocarbons of different chain lengths, which is why it can be separated physically by fractional distillation.

questions.stem: Fractional distillation separates petroleum into fractions because the different hydrocarbons have different:
questions.explanation: The column is hot at the bottom and cool at the top, so each fraction condenses at the height matching its boiling point. It is a physical separation based on boiling point differences.

questions.stem: Which fraction of petroleum is used as fuel for jet aircraft?
questions.explanation: Kerosene (paraffin) is the jet fuel fraction. Diesel powers diesel engines, refinery gas is bottled for heating and cooking, and bitumen surfaces roads.

questions.stem: A new fraction is collected from NEAR THE TOP of a fractionating column. Which properties is it most likely to have?
choices: High boiling point, high viscosity, long-chain molecules
Low boiling point, high volatility, short-chain molecules
Low boiling point, high viscosity, long-chain molecules
High boiling point, low volatility, short-chain molecules
questions.explanation: From bottom to top of the column, boiling point, viscosity and chain length all decrease while volatility increases. A top fraction therefore has short chains, a low boiling point and high volatility.

questions.stem: Which fraction of petroleum is used for surfacing roads?
questions.explanation: Bitumen, the thick residue from the bottom of the column, is used to surface roads. Naphtha is the chemical-industry feedstock and fuel oil powers ships and heating systems.

questions.stem: A gas heater burns methane in a poorly ventilated room. Why is this dangerous?
choices: Complete combustion releases too much energy for the room
The methane reacts with nitrogen in the air to form ammonia
Limited oxygen causes incomplete combustion, producing toxic carbon monoxide
The water vapour produced damages the lungs
questions.explanation: With a limited oxygen supply the carbon is only partly oxidised, so carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide. CO is colourless and odourless and binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport in the blood.

questions.stem: What are the products of the complete combustion of any hydrocarbon in a plentiful supply of oxygen?
questions.explanation: Complete combustion fully oxidises the carbon to CO₂ and the hydrogen to H₂O. Carbon monoxide or soot appear only when oxygen is limited, and hydrogen gas is never a combustion product.

questions.stem: Which statement about cracking is correct?
choices: Long-chain alkanes are broken down by a heated catalyst into shorter alkanes and alkenes
Small alkene molecules are joined together to make long-chain alkanes
Petroleum is separated into fractions using a heated catalyst
Alkanes react with bromine water to form alkenes
questions.explanation: Cracking uses a heated catalyst to break long-chain alkane molecules into a shorter alkane plus an alkene, meeting the demand for petrol and for alkene feedstock. Joining small molecules is polymerisation, and separating petroleum is fractional distillation.

questions.stem: A colourless hydrocarbon is shaken with orange bromine water and the mixture turns colourless. What does this show?
choices: The hydrocarbon contains a C=C double bond — it is unsaturated
The hydrocarbon is a carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Bromine adds across a C=C double bond and is used up, so the orange colour disappears. A saturated alkane would leave the bromine water orange, and a carboxylic acid is not a hydrocarbon.

questions.stem: Propane burns completely in oxygen: C₃H₈ + xO₂ → yCO₂ + zH₂O. What are the correct values of x, y and z?
questions.explanation: Balance the carbons first (y = 3 CO₂), then the hydrogens (8 H gives z = 4 H₂O), then count oxygens on the right: (3 × 2) + 4 = 10, so x = 5 O₂. The balanced equation is C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
